events.title: Monteverdi's Orfeo Premieres
events.blurb: A 39-year-old Italian composer staged a setting of the Orpheus myth at a ducal palace in a northern Italian city, combining recitative, arias, choruses, and instrumental ritornellos in a way earlier experimental works had only gestured at. The resulting five-act piece is considered the first opera that remains in the regular performance repertoire. Only two printed scores of the work survive.
events.revealBlurb: February 24, 1607 — Claudio Monteverdi at the court of the Gonzagas in Mantua. The orchestra called for some 40 instruments. The character of Orpheus was sung by tenor Francesco Rasi; the audience was tiny — members of the Accademia degli Invaghiti.

events.title: The Rite of Spring Riot
events.blurb: A 30-year-old Russian composer's ballet score, depicting a pagan spring ritual with jagged rhythms, dissonant chord stacks, and primitivist choreography, premiered at a new Paris theatre and nearly caused a full-scale audience riot. Shouts, whistles, and fistfights broke out within minutes; the choreographer had to shout counts to dancers from the wings because they couldn't hear the orchestra. The piece is now considered one of the pivotal works of 20th-century music.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1913 — Igor Stravinsky and Ballets Russes at Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, Paris. Choreography by Vaslav Nijinsky. The Parisian critic Carl Van Vechten reported his seat-neighbour beating rhythmically on his head with his fists in distress.

events.title: Dylan Goes Electric
events.blurb: A 24-year-old folk singer, backed by a ragged rhythm section from the previous night's acquaintance, walked onto the stage of a folk festival on a Rhode Island pier with a sunburst Stratocaster slung low over his shoulder. He played three short electric songs before some boos drowned out the applause. He walked off, returned with his acoustic, and played two more. The event marked, depending on who tells it, the birth of folk-rock or the betrayal of American folk.
events.revealBlurb: July 25, 1965 — Bob Dylan at the Newport Folk Festival. Pete Seeger, legend says, tried to cut the sound cables with an axe. Seeger later denied it. The songs included "Maggie's Farm" and "Like a Rolling Stone." Dylan's next tour was booed nightly for a year.

events.title: Woodstock Festival Opens
events.blurb: A music festival on a dairy farm in upstate New York that had sold 186,000 advance tickets was overwhelmed by more than 400,000 attendees in the preceding 48 hours, forcing organisers to declare it a free event and abandon the ticket booths. Thirty-two acts performed over four rain-soaked days, and the festival became the defining cultural gathering of its generation.

events.title: MTV Launches
events.blurb: A new American cable channel devoted entirely to music videos went on the air at one minute past midnight Eastern time with a countdown, a rocket, and a footage loop of the Apollo 11 moon landing with the channel's logo hoisted as a flag. The first music video it played was a novelty track by a British synth-pop group with a prescient title. Within four years it had reshaped the music industry's priorities and, quite possibly, a generation's attention span.
events.revealBlurb: August 1, 1981 — Music Television. First video: "Video Killed the Radio Star" by the Buggles. The channel ran music videos almost exclusively until the late 1990s; today it runs reality programming and airs barely any music.

events.title: Cyrus the Great Takes Babylon
events.blurb: A Persian king who had already conquered Media, Lydia, and the Ionian cities entered the ancient city of Babylon without a fight, claiming to have been welcomed by its priests as the rightful king of the gods. His subsequent proclamation — known from a surviving cuneiform cylinder — repatriated exiled populations, restored local temples, and is sometimes described as the oldest surviving charter of human rights. The Persian Achaemenid Empire he founded became the largest the world had yet seen.
events.revealBlurb: October 29, 539 BCE — Cyrus II. The Cyrus Cylinder is now in the British Museum. The Hebrew Bible credits Cyrus with allowing the Judean exiles to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple; he is the only non-Jewish figure called "messiah" in the Hebrew scriptures.

events.title: Battle of Chaeronea
events.blurb: A Macedonian king's army of 32,000 defeated a combined Athenian-Theban force of similar size in central Greece, ending the independence of the classical Greek city-states. The victor's 18-year-old son, commanding the Macedonian left wing, personally broke the famous Sacred Band of Thebes — a unit of 300 elite warrior-lovers who died to the man. The defeat of the city-states unified Greece under Macedonian hegemony and set up the Asian conquests that would follow.
events.revealBlurb: August 338 BCE — King Philip II and his son Alexander. The Sacred Band of Thebes had won every battle it had fought for 40 years; it lost only at Chaeronea. Philip erected a stone lion over their mass grave; the lion, damaged over millennia, was restored in 1902 and still stands there.

events.title: Hannibal Crosses the Alps
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Carthaginian general marched an army of 50,000 men, 9,000 cavalry, and 37 war elephants from Iberia over the Alps into northern Italy over 15 days of early winter, intending to take the war to Rome's home territory. Half his men died in the crossing from cold, hunger, and hostile Alpine tribes. The force that did make it to Italy shocked Rome by winning three successive battles within two years, annihilating Roman legions at Trebbia, Lake Trasimene, and Cannae.
events.revealBlurb: 218 BCE — Hannibal Barca. The exact Alpine pass he used is still debated; the leading candidates are the Col de la Traversette or the Col du Mont Cenis. Only a few elephants made it across and most died in Italy's wet winter. Hannibal won tactically but could not take Rome itself.

events.title: Battle of Adrianople
events.blurb: After Rome settled Visigothic refugees south of the Danube and then systematically starved and abused them, the Goths rose in revolt. Emperor Valens — who refused to wait for reinforcements — attacked their fortified camp with approximately 30,000 men. Gothic cavalry flanked both sides of the Roman line and trapped the legions; two-thirds of the eastern field army was destroyed and Valens himself was killed.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 378 CE. Valens's body was never found. One account says he was carried wounded to a farmhouse, which Gothic soldiers then set alight; another says he was lost in the general slaughter. Military historians sometimes call Adrianople "the ancient world's Stalingrad."

events.title: Fall of Constantinople
events.blurb: An Ottoman sultan, 21 years old, directed a 53-day siege of the Byzantine capital with 80,000 troops, an army of miners who tunneled under the walls, and enormous bronze cannons that fired 550-kilogram stone balls. The last Roman emperor died fighting at a breach in his city's walls. The 1,100-year-old Byzantine state, the direct legal continuation of Roman rule, ended.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1453 — Mehmed II. The city's Greek name, Constantinople, stayed in formal Ottoman use until 1930; "Istanbul" is how Byzantine Greeks had always said "to the city" colloquially. Hagia Sophia became a mosque that Friday.

events.title: Babe Ruth Sold to Yankees
events.blurb: A Boston baseball team's owner, needing cash to finance a Broadway musical he had invested in, sold the star pitcher and outfielder of his defending World Series champion team to the rival New York franchise for $100,000 cash plus a $300,000 loan secured by the team's stadium. The deal shipped the best player in baseball to the Yankees; Boston did not win another World Series for 86 years. Yankee championships followed in a cascade.
events.revealBlurb: January 3, 1920 — Red Sox owner Harry Frazee sold Ruth to the Yankees. The musical was "No, No, Nanette" (1925); its eventual success does not redeem the sale. Ruth would hit 714 career home runs, lead the Yankees to 7 pennants, and define American sport for a generation.

events.title: Jesse Owens Wins First Berlin Gold
events.blurb: An American sprinter from Alabama won the first of four gold medals at the Berlin Summer Games, finishing the 100-metre dash in 10.3 seconds before 110,000 spectators. He went on to win gold in the 200 metres, long jump, and 4×100-metre relay — shattering the narrative that the host nation's athletes would dominate.

events.title: Jesse Owens at Berlin Olympics
events.blurb: A 22-year-old African-American sprinter won four gold medals at a Summer Olympics held in the capital of a regime that had publicly declared the inferiority of his race. He took the 100m (10.3), 200m (20.7), long jump (8.06m), and 4×100m relay. His performance personally refuted Nazi racial theorizing on a stage the regime had built for its own glorification. He was welcomed home with a ticker-tape parade through New York but had to ride a freight elevator at his own Waldorf-Astoria reception because Black guests were not permitted in the main elevators.
events.revealBlurb: August 3-9, 1936 — Jesse Owens. The story that Hitler refused to shake his hand is disputed; Hitler had stopped shaking any medal winners' hands after the first day. President Roosevelt never congratulated Owens; Owens said later: "Hitler didn't snub me — it was our president who snubbed me."

events.title: The Rumble in the Jungle
events.blurb: A 32-year-old heavyweight boxing challenger, widely predicted to lose to the younger and vastly more powerful champion, leaned back against the ropes for seven rounds and absorbed punishing body blows — a tactic he later nicknamed "rope-a-dope." In the 8th, when the champion visibly tired, the challenger delivered a flurry of punches that knocked him out. The fight was held in an African capital as part of a pioneering pan-African promotion.
events.revealBlurb: October 30, 1974 — Muhammad Ali KO'd George Foreman at the Stade du 20 Mai in Kinshasa, Zaire (now Democratic Republic of the Congo). Promoter Don King organized it. The event was immortalized in the 1996 documentary "When We Were Kings."

events.title: Kobe Bryant Dies
events.blurb: A 41-year-old retired basketball star, his 13-year-old daughter, and seven other passengers died when their private helicopter crashed into a hillside in thick fog outside Los Angeles while en route to a youth basketball game. The retired player had won five NBA championships, two Olympic golds, and the nickname "Black Mamba" during a 20-year career entirely with the Los Angeles Lakers. The crash prompted an outpouring of mourning around the world.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 2020 — Kobe and Gianna Bryant. National Transportation Safety Board findings attributed the crash to pilot error in poor visibility. His 2017 jersey-retirement ceremony at Staples Center saw both his numbers (8 and 24) raised to the rafters — the only player in franchise history with multiple retired numbers.

events.title: Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact
events.blurb: Two ideologically opposed dictatorships stunned the world by signing a non-aggression treaty after midnight in a capital city, including a secret clause dividing neighbouring countries into separate spheres of influence like cuts of a butchered animal. Every government in Europe recalculated its position by morning.
events.revealBlurb: Signed August 23, 1939 in Moscow. The secret protocol carved up Poland, Finland, the Baltic states, and Romania between Germany and the USSR — without telling any of those countries. Stalin was so pleased he personally opened champagne. The pact lasted exactly 22 months.

events.title: Lend-Lease Act Signed
events.blurb: A nation officially at peace passed legislation allowing its president to lend, lease, or otherwise transfer war materials to any country whose defence he deemed vital to national security, bypassing a strict neutrality law without technically entering the conflict. The first shipments moved within weeks, directed at an island nation running critically short of everything.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 1941 — FDR signed H.R. 1776 (the bill number was a deliberate wink). By the end of the programme, the US had shipped $50 billion in supplies — equivalent to roughly $800 billion today — to 38 countries. The Soviet Union received about 17 million tons of equipment, including 400,000 jeeps and trucks.

events.title: Fall of Tobruk
events.blurb: A fortified port city that had withstood a nine-month siege the previous year fell to an armoured assault in a single day, yielding 33,000 prisoners — including an entire South African division — along with 2,000 vehicles, 5,000 tons of food, and enough fuel to sustain the attacking force's advance for weeks.
events.revealBlurb: June 21, 1942. Churchill learned of Tobruk's fall while meeting Roosevelt in Washington — handed a pink slip of paper mid-meeting. Roosevelt's immediate response: "What can we do to help?" He arranged 300 Sherman tanks and 100 self-propelled guns for immediate shipment. The news triggered a no-confidence vote against Churchill in the House of Commons.

events.title: Atomic Bombing of Hiroshima
events.blurb: A single aircraft flying at high altitude released a single bomb over a mid-sized city at 8:15 in the morning, detonating it 600 metres above a distinctive T-shaped bridge with the force of 15,000 tons of TNT — flattening 13 square kilometres, killing between 70,000 and 80,000 people instantly, and ultimately causing 140,000 deaths by the end of the year.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 1945 — B-29 Enola Gay, piloted by Colonel Paul Tibbets, dropped "Little Boy" over Hiroshima. The aiming point was the Aioi Bridge. The bomb missed by about 250 metres but it did not matter. Tibbets's mother's name was Enola Gay. The co-pilot, Robert Lewis, wrote in his journal: "My God, what have we done?"

events.title: Atomic Bombing of Nagasaki
events.blurb: A second atomic strike, delivered three days after the first, detonated with the force of 22,000 tons of TNT over a city's industrial valley — but cloud cover over the primary target had forced the bomber to divert to its secondary, sparing one city and condemning another, while a city 160 kilometres away had been removed from the target list weeks earlier at the personal request of the American Secretary of War.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1945 — the B-29 Bockscar dropped "Fat Man" at 11:02 AM. Kokura, the original target, was obscured by clouds; pilot Sweeney diverted to Nagasaki. An estimated 40,000 died instantly; 80,000 total by year's end. Secretary of War Stimson had personally removed Kyoto from the target list because he had visited it on his honeymoon and loved it.

events.title: Watt's Separate Condenser
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Scottish instrument maker, repairing a model of a 50-year-old atmospheric engine for a university natural philosophy class, realized its efficiency was fatally compromised by repeatedly heating and cooling the same cylinder. His solution — a separate condensing vessel — cut fuel consumption by 75 percent. Patented four years later, the improved engine could be sited anywhere, not only beside a coal pit, and became the prime mover of 19th-century industry.
events.revealBlurb: 1765 insight; January 5, 1769 patent — James Watt. His decade-long partnership with Birmingham industrialist Matthew Boulton commercialized the engine. The unit of power is named for him. "Horsepower" was also his invention, a marketing metric.

events.title: First Transatlantic Telegraph Cable
events.blurb: After two previous attempts failed mid-Atlantic, a joint American-British consortium successfully laid a 3,700-kilometre copper cable across the ocean floor between Ireland and Newfoundland. The Queen of England and the President of the United States exchanged the first messages. The cable's signal degraded rapidly — the 99-word inaugural message took 17 hours to send — and the cable failed entirely within three weeks, but the feasibility had been proved.
events.revealBlurb: August 5, 1858 — the cable was completed; August 16, the first messages between Queen Victoria and President James Buchanan. The project's main backer, American financier Cyrus West Field, persisted through four failed attempts and finally established a durable cable in 1866. His Atlantic cables cut communication between continents from weeks to minutes.

events.title: Suez Canal Opens
events.blurb: The French-designed 193-kilometre sea-level canal linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea — dug largely by corvée (unpaid forced) Egyptian labour over ten years with massive loss of life — opened to international traffic. A procession of 68 ships led by a French imperial yacht sailed from Port Said to the Red Sea over four days. The canal cut the sea route from London to Bombay by about 7,200 kilometres and shifted the geography of global trade.
events.revealBlurb: November 17, 1869 — designer Ferdinand de Lesseps. Giuseppe Verdi's opera Aida, commissioned by Khedive Ismail for the opening, arrived too late and premiered in 1871. The canal was nationalized by Egypt in 1956, triggering the Suez Crisis.

events.title: Coca-Cola Invented
events.blurb: An Atlanta pharmacist, a former Confederate officer who had become addicted to morphine following a Civil War injury, mixed a flavoured syrup of coca leaves and kola nuts with carbonated water at a downtown soda fountain and began selling it by the glass as a "brain tonic." The formula initially contained a small amount of cocaine; it was removed in 1903. The modestly popular local beverage grew into the world's most recognized consumer brand.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1886 — John Pemberton at Jacobs' Pharmacy, Atlanta. Pemberton sold the formula piecemeal in ill health; Asa Griggs Candler consolidated ownership and built the business. Coca-Cola's secret recipe, "Merchandise 7X," is supposedly known to only two executives at any time.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: Parthenon Marbles Completed
events.blurb: Under the direction of a single master sculptor, a team of Athenian craftsmen completed the exterior sculptural programme of a temple on a fortified limestone hill above their city — a continuous carved frieze 160 metres long depicting a civic religious procession, plus 92 metopes and two pediments. The sculptures were painted in vivid colours; the bleached white appearance known to modern viewers is an accident of weathering.
events.revealBlurb: c. 438 BCE — Phidias, chief sculptor of the Parthenon in Athens. Lord Elgin removed about half the surviving marbles between 1801 and 1812 and sold them to the British Museum. Greece has been asking for them back for over 200 years.

events.title: Michelangelo's David Unveiled
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Florentine sculptor unveiled a 5.17-metre marble nude of a biblical hero, carved over three years from a single block of Carrara marble that had been rejected by two earlier sculptors as flawed. The statue was intended for the rooftop of a cathedral; a committee that included Leonardo da Vinci decided the work was too significant to put out of sight and instead installed it in the main square of the city.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1504 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. Moving it from the workshop to the Piazza della Signoria took 40 men 4 days. The statue was damaged by a mob in 1527 and by a 1991 attack with a hammer; it now stands indoors at the Accademia, where a copy watches over the piazza.

events.title: Raphael's School of Athens
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Umbrian painter completed the second of four monumental frescoes on the walls of the pope's private library at the Vatican, gathering the giants of classical philosophy into a single imaginary architectural space. Plato and Aristotle walk forward from a vanishing point; Pythagoras writes in a book, Euclid draws on a slate, Heraclitus leans alone on a block. The face of Euclid is the architect Bramante; Heraclitus is Michelangelo, working bitterly next door.
events.revealBlurb: 1511 — Raphael Sanzio, in the Stanza della Segnatura. The rivalry with Michelangelo, then painting the Sistine Ceiling a short walk away, was real; Raphael added him as an afterthought in a late revision.

events.title: Leonardo da Vinci Dies
events.blurb: A 67-year-old Florentine polymath died in a small château in the Loire Valley, where the French king had invited him to retire. On the easel beside his bed was an unfinished portrait of a Florentine merchant's wife that he had carried with him for sixteen years and never delivered to the man who had commissioned it. The king would acquire the painting from his executor; the subject's name, Lisa Gherardini, would eventually become the most famous name in art.
events.revealBlurb: May 2, 1519 — Leonardo at Clos Lucé, Amboise. The portrait is the Mona Lisa, now in the Louvre, which he had begun around 1503. He bequeathed his notebooks, which he wrote in mirror script, to his assistant Francesco Melzi.

events.title: Artemisia Gentileschi's Judith
events.blurb: A Roman painter in her mid-twenties completed a large oil on canvas of a biblical heroine and her maidservant beheading an Assyrian general — a scene painted by many male artists before her, but never this physically, with two women straining against the weight of the act and blood spraying across the sheets. The painter had been raped and then tortured with thumbscrews during the trial of her rapist seven years earlier; the subject matter was not accidental.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1620 — Artemisia Gentileschi. Now in Naples' Museo di Capodimonte. An earlier version she painted between 1611 and 1613 hangs in Florence's Uffizi. Gentileschi became the first woman admitted to Florence's Accademia delle Arti del Disegno.

events.title: British Parliament Passes the Stamp Act
events.blurb: Parliament enacted a sweeping tax requiring colonists to purchase revenue stamps for newspapers, legal documents, almanacs, and even playing cards — the first direct tax Britain had ever levied on its American colonies. Outcry was immediate and visceral: colonial assemblies passed resolutions of protest, merchants organized boycotts, and a new network of radicals calling themselves the Sons of Liberty took to the streets.
events.revealBlurb: March 22, 1765 — London. The tax was repealed the following year under merchant pressure, but Parliament simultaneously passed the Declaratory Act asserting its absolute right to tax the colonies "in all cases whatsoever." The colonists celebrated the repeal and mostly ignored the Declaratory Act — for about a decade.

events.title: Marbury v. Madison: Judicial Review Established
events.blurb: Chief Justice John Marshall wrote the unanimous Supreme Court opinion in a case about a disputed judicial appointment, using it to announce that federal courts possessed the power to strike down laws they found incompatible with the Constitution — a power the Constitution itself does not explicitly mention. The ruling transformed the Supreme Court from the weakest branch of government into an equal arbiter of constitutional meaning.
events.revealBlurb: February 24, 1803 — Washington, D.C. Marshall's genius was ruling against Marbury (who wanted his commission) so Jefferson couldn't refuse to comply, while simultaneously claiming the Court's enormous new power. Jefferson privately hated the decision but was trapped. The ruling wasn't used to strike down another law for 54 more years.

events.title: Caning of Senator Charles Sumner
events.blurb: Representative Preston Brooks of South Carolina strode onto the Senate floor and beat Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts unconscious with a metal-topped gutta-percha cane, inflicting such severe head injuries that Sumner could not return to his seat for over three years. The assault came two days after Sumner delivered a blistering antislavery speech mocking Brooks's cousin; Massachusetts left Sumner's empty desk on display as a rebuke.
events.revealBlurb: May 22, 1856 — U.S. Senate chamber. Brooks resigned, was immediately re-elected by South Carolina, and received commemorative canes inscribed "Hit Him Again." Sumner's empty desk served as visible propaganda for the antislavery cause for three years. The incident convinced many Northerners that slavery corrupted men beyond reason.

events.title: Atomic Bomb Dropped on Hiroshima
events.blurb: At 8:15 that morning, a B-29 Superfortress named the Enola Gay released a uranium bomb nicknamed "Little Boy" over the Japanese city of Hiroshima, which detonated at 1,968 feet above the city center with a force equivalent to approximately 15,000 tons of TNT. Estimates of deaths in the four months following the explosion range from 90,000 to 166,000; roughly two-thirds of the city's buildings were destroyed.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 1945 — Hiroshima, Japan. "Little Boy" was the first nuclear weapon ever used in warfare, but it had never been fully tested — scientists were confident enough in the gun-type design. Japan did not surrender after Hiroshima; it took a second bomb (Nagasaki, August 9) to produce the surrender announcement.

events.title: Nixon Resigns the Presidency
events.blurb: That evening, Richard Nixon became the first and only U.S. president to resign from office, delivering a nationally televised address from the Oval Office in which he announced his departure would take effect at noon the following day. The resignation came after the release of the "smoking gun" tape proved Nixon had personally directed the Watergate cover-up six days after the break-in, making his impeachment and Senate conviction certain.
events.revealBlurb: August 8, 1974 — The Oval Office. Nixon's approval rating the week of his resignation was 24%. Gerald Ford pardoned him one month later, saying "our long national nightmare is over" — a pardon that likely cost Ford the 1976 election. Nixon is the only president ever to resign.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.

events.title: Fall of Tenochtitlán
events.blurb: After a three-month siege — during which Spanish-allied Indigenous forces demolished the city district by district, channeled the causeways, and introduced a devastating smallpox epidemic — the last Aztec emperor surrendered in a canoe on the lake as his capital burned. The Spaniards, led by Cortés, renamed the ruins and built a viceregal capital on them. The Aztec empire ceased to exist; the Spanish conquest of the Americas was underway.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1521 — Cuauhtémoc surrendered to Cortés. The city's population had dropped from perhaps 200,000 to under 50,000 through disease, siege starvation, and fighting. The Spanish built Mexico City on the drained lakebed — which continues to sink today at 50 cm per year.

events.title: Spanish Armada Defeated
events.blurb: A Spanish naval force of 130 ships and 26,000 men, intended to escort a Flemish invasion army across the Channel to England, was met by a faster, more maneuverable English fleet off the Flanders coast. An English fireship attack scattered the Spanish anchorage overnight; the following day's running battle crippled the armada. Storms in the North Sea and along the Irish coast destroyed the rest on the long retreat home. Barely half returned to Spain.
events.revealBlurb: July 29 to August 8, 1588 — Battle of Gravelines decided it. English commanders: Lord Howard of Effingham, Sir Francis Drake. Roughly 35 Spanish ships reached home; most of the rest were wrecked on the Irish coast, whose people dealt harshly with survivors.

events.title: Shakespeare's First Folio
events.blurb: Seven years after the Stratford-born playwright's death, two of his fellow actors compiled and published a folio edition of 36 of his plays — 18 of which had never been printed before. Without the volume, half the plays, including Macbeth, Julius Caesar, and The Tempest, would have been lost. 750 copies were printed; 235 are known to survive today, fetching tens of millions at auction.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1623 — compiled by John Heminges and Henry Condell. It was sold for £1 — roughly £200 today. A recently discovered copy was unmasked at a Scottish library in 2016. The folio standardized the canonical text of most of the plays.

events.title: Peace of Westphalia
events.blurb: Two treaties negotiated simultaneously at two Westphalian cities ended the Thirty Years War in Germany and the Eighty Years War between Spain and the Dutch Republic. 235 delegations from across Europe had been meeting for four years. The settlement recognized the sovereign equality of European states, gave rulers the right to determine the religion of their own territories, and acknowledged Dutch and Swiss independence. Historians often date the modern state system from here.
events.revealBlurb: October 24, 1648 — treaties signed at Münster and Osnabrück. The war had killed an estimated eight million people, roughly 20 percent of the German population. The phrase "Westphalian sovereignty" still refers to the principle of non-intervention in internal affairs of other states.

events.title: Great Pyramid of Giza Completed
events.blurb: A vast limestone monument covering 5.3 hectares and rising 146 metres — the tallest man-made structure for 3,800 years — was completed as the royal tomb of the second king of Egypt's Fourth Dynasty. It consists of 2.3 million blocks, each weighing 2.5 tonnes on average, quarried from nearby escarpments and shipped down the Nile. Some 20,000 paid labourers — not slaves, as was long assumed — built it in roughly twenty years.
events.revealBlurb: c. 2560 BCE — Pharaoh Khufu (Cheops). It was originally clad in smooth white limestone, robbed mostly in medieval times for Cairo construction. Its internal geometry — chambers, passages, "air shafts" — continues to attract theorizing. It is the last surviving "Seven Wonders of the Ancient World."

events.title: Pont du Gard Built
events.blurb: A three-tiered limestone aqueduct bridge was constructed to carry water 50 kilometres across southern Gaul to the Roman colony of Nemausus (modern Nîmes). The top level — 48 metres above the River Gard — still carried its channel; the whole structure spans 275 metres. It was built dry, without mortar, using stones so precisely cut that the joints remain watertight after two millennia. The aqueduct itself was decommissioned in the 6th century; the bridge survived as a road crossing.
events.revealBlurb: c. 50 CE — built under Emperor Claudius. The water it carried had a gradient of only 1 in 3,000 — about 30 centimetres of drop per kilometre. The Pont du Gard is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most visited tourist destinations in France.

events.title: Leaning Tower of Pisa Begun
events.blurb: Construction began on a free-standing bell tower for the cathedral complex of an Italian city-state on the Tuscan coast. By the time three of its eight stories were finished five years later, the soft alluvial ground beneath the south side was already sinking noticeably. Construction was halted for nearly a century. When work resumed, builders attempted to compensate by building upper floors taller on the low side — so the tower is actually curved. It was completed 199 years after ground-breaking.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1173 — Pisa Cathedral bell tower. The tilt is currently about 3.97 degrees after stabilization work completed in 2008. Galileo is said to have dropped balls of different weights from it to demonstrate they fall at the same rate — the story is almost certainly apocryphal.

events.title: Panama Canal Opens
events.blurb: A 77-kilometre canal cutting across the narrowest part of the Central American isthmus opened to international shipping, after a US-run construction effort that had finished a French attempt abandoned two decades earlier amid malaria, yellow fever, and bankruptcy. The canal used a system of locks to raise ships 26 metres above sea level across the continental divide. It cut the sea route from New York to San Francisco by over 12,000 kilometres.
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1914 — the ship SS Ancon made the first full transit. The American construction was made possible partly by controlling yellow fever and malaria through mosquito eradication. The 1977 Torrijos-Carter treaties returned the canal to Panamanian sovereignty in 1999.

events.title: Chrysler Building Completed
events.blurb: A 319-metre Manhattan skyscraper, topped with a radiator-cap-inspired sunburst spire, opened at the corner of 42nd Street and Lexington Avenue as the tallest building in the world. Its automotive-magnate patron had kept the spire a construction secret; it was assembled inside the tower's upper levels and then hoisted into place in 90 minutes, triumphing over a rival bank project down Wall Street that had briefly claimed the height title. The Empire State Building eclipsed it 11 months later.
events.revealBlurb: May 27, 1930 — architect William Van Alen for Walter Chrysler. The Art Deco ornamentation includes eagle gargoyles at the 61st floor and a 1,700-square-metre ceiling mural in the lobby. Van Alen was never paid his fee — Chrysler accused him of taking bribes from suppliers.

events.title: Battle of Tours
events.blurb: A Frankish mayor of the palace led an infantry army into a defensive wall of shields against a much larger Umayyad cavalry force that had been raiding deep into western Europe. The battle's outcome stopped the northward expansion of the Islamic caliphate into the Frankish heartland and established the Carolingian dynasty as the dominant power of the region.
events.revealBlurb: October 10, 732 — Charles Martel ("Charles the Hammer") in central France. His grandson Charlemagne would be crowned emperor 68 years later. Edward Gibbon later wrote that without the victory, "the interpretation of the Koran would now be taught in the schools of Oxford."

events.title: Treaty of Verdun
events.blurb: Three grandsons of Charlemagne, after a three-year civil war, signed a treaty in a French town dividing their grandfather's empire into three kingdoms — a western Frankish one destined to become France, an eastern one destined to become Germany, and a middle strip whose ownership would be disputed for a thousand years.
events.revealBlurb: August 843 — Louis the German got the east, Charles the Bald got the west, Lothair got the middle (Lotharingia, surviving in "Lorraine"). The France–Germany border problem is essentially a 1,200-year-old inheritance dispute.

events.title: Magna Carta Sealed
events.blurb: Facing armed revolt by his barons after a series of disastrous foreign wars and arbitrary taxation, an English king met them in a meadow beside the Thames and affixed his seal to a 63-clause charter limiting royal power, guaranteeing trial by peers, and making free men subject only to "the law of the land." He repudiated it within ten weeks; civil war resumed.
events.revealBlurb: June 15, 1215 — King John at Runnymede. Only three original copies survive. Clauses against arbitrary imprisonment echo today through American due-process law. The barons were self-interested, not democratic, but the language was universal enough to outlive them.

events.title: Marco Polo Departs for China
events.blurb: A 17-year-old Venetian merchant's son set out with his father and uncle on a journey across Asia to the court of the Mongol emperor. He would return to Venice 24 years later and, captured in a war with Genoa three years after that, dictate an account of his travels to a cellmate. The resulting book became the most influential western description of Asia for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 1271 — Marco left Venice with Niccolò and Maffeo Polo. Returning in 1295, he was imprisoned by the Genoese; his cellmate Rustichello da Pisa helped him write "Il Milione." Christopher Columbus's annotated copy survives.

events.title: Battle of Agincourt
events.blurb: An exhausted English army, heavily outnumbered, caught in thick mud on a narrow front between two woods in northern France, stood behind sharpened wooden stakes and cut down the armored flower of French nobility with longbows at point-blank range. The French dead included a constable, three dukes, and over 1,500 knights; English losses were perhaps 400. Shakespeare would turn it into a speech 180 years later.
events.revealBlurb: October 25, 1415 — Henry V on St. Crispin's Day. Henry ordered the slaughter of prisoners mid-battle when he feared a rear attack; this remains controversial. The longbow's armor-piercing arrowheads were called "bodkins."

events.title: American Idol Premieres
events.blurb: A singing-competition reality show — adapted from a British format — premiered on Fox with a caustic British music executive as its lead judge, flanked by two milder American ones. The first season's audition rounds and final contestant-viewer-vote format drew enormous audiences; its first winner, a 20-year-old Texan waitress, became a genuine pop star. The show's stern British judge became a cultural shorthand for merciless critique.
events.revealBlurb: June 11, 2002 — judges Simon Cowell, Paula Abdul, Randy Jackson. Host Ryan Seacrest. Season 1 winner Kelly Clarkson went on to a successful music and TV career. American Idol ran on Fox until 2016 and was revived on ABC in 2018; Clarkson's "A Moment Like This" is still its most famous product.

events.title: Michael Jackson Dies
events.blurb: A 50-year-old American singer widely regarded as the most successful pop star of his generation died of cardiac arrest at his rented Los Angeles home while preparing for a 50-concert comeback tour in London. His personal physician was later convicted of involuntary manslaughter for administering propofol, a surgical anesthetic, to help him sleep. His death prompted an outpouring of grief that crashed major websites and sold over 35 million of his records in the following six months.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 2009 — Michael Jackson. His physician, Conrad Murray, was sentenced to 4 years and served 2. His public memorial on July 7 drew 31 million U.S. TV viewers. The "This Is It" concert film, compiled from rehearsal footage, grossed $261 million posthumously.

events.title: Balloon Boy Hoax
events.blurb: A Colorado family reported that their 6-year-old son had been carried aloft in a homemade silver mylar weather balloon that had drifted off from their backyard. National news networks covered the balloon's two-hour, 80-kilometre flight live, interrupting regular programming. The balloon landed empty. The boy was found hiding in the family attic. Within a day, the father admitted the whole thing had been a publicity stunt, hoping to land the family a reality-TV show.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 2009 — Heene family, Fort Collins, CO. The father Richard Heene was convicted of a felony and served 30 days; the mother Mayumi got misdemeanor charges. The Heenes reportedly received a pardon from Colorado governor Jared Polis in December 2020.

events.title: Robin Williams Dies
events.blurb: A 63-year-old American actor and comedian was found dead at his home in California's Marin County, having died by suicide. An autopsy later revealed he had been suffering from Lewy body dementia — a form of dementia that causes visual hallucinations and movement problems — that had been misdiagnosed as Parkinson's disease during his lifetime. His widow wrote afterwards that the real disease had been terrifying him; she called it "the terrorist in my husband's brain."
events.revealBlurb: August 11, 2014 — Robin Williams. His final film "Night at the Museum: Secret of the Tomb" was released posthumously in December. Williams had won an Academy Award for "Good Will Hunting" (1997); his improvised standup, Mork & Mindy, Mrs. Doubtfire, Aladdin, and Dead Poets Society span a career of enormous generosity toward audiences.

events.title: Hamilton Opens on Broadway
events.blurb: A hip-hop-based musical about the founding-era American politician Alexander Hamilton, written by a 35-year-old playwright-composer who had performed an early version at a White House poetry event in 2009, opened on Broadway after a sold-out off-Broadway run. The show's casting of non-white actors as the Founding Fathers, its rapid-fire rap-through-historical-politics, and its grand storytelling about ambition and legacy made it a generational phenomenon. Tickets sold on the secondary market for over $1,000.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 2015 — Lin-Manuel Miranda as Hamilton at the Richard Rodgers Theatre. The show won 11 Tony Awards in 2016 and a Pulitzer Prize for Drama. A professionally filmed version premiered on Disney+ on July 3, 2020 during the COVID pandemic, drawing enormous viewership.

events.title: IBM Personal Computer Launched
events.blurb: A technology corporation released a personal computer based on an Intel processor running an operating system licensed from a small software company for $25,000. Its open architecture allowed third-party manufacturers to build compatible clones, spawning a global personal computer industry worth trillions within a decade.

events.title: IBM PC Released
events.blurb: The world's dominant mainframe computer maker released a small desktop machine built, unusually for the company, from off-the-shelf parts — an Intel 8088 processor, an operating system licensed from Microsoft, components any competitor could buy. Business customers trusted the name and bought millions. The design's open specifications led to a decade of "IBM compatible" clones that collectively made the Intel/Microsoft duopoly inevitable.
events.revealBlurb: August 12, 1981 — IBM PC model 5150. It had 16KB of RAM and no hard drive. IBM's decision to source DOS from Microsoft, rather than write it in-house, is usually cited as the great strategic error of 20th-century computing. Gates retained all distribution rights.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: AlphaGo Beats Lee Sedol
events.blurb: A London-based artificial intelligence laboratory's go-playing program, trained on millions of human games and then on games it had played against itself, defeated the reigning world champion of the ancient Asian board game 4–1 in a five-game match in Seoul. The match was broadcast live to 280 million people. Experts had predicted a champion-beating go program was a decade away; the algorithmic gap between games like chess and go had seemed insurmountable.
events.revealBlurb: March 15, 2016 — DeepMind's AlphaGo vs. Lee Sedol. Lee's single winning game, move 78 — the "divine move" — exploited a subtle blind spot in the AI. DeepMind was acquired by Google in 2014 for around $500 million. Lee retired from professional go three years later, partly because AI had changed the game.

events.title: Apple M1 Chip Released
events.blurb: A California computer company released the first Mac laptops powered by a chip it had designed in-house, based on the ARM instruction set. The M1 provided substantially better performance per watt than the Intel chips Apple had shipped in Macs for 15 years. Reviews were rapturous; the company would completely abandon Intel chips across its laptop and desktop lines within two years. The industry's Intel-based personal-computer architecture lost a long-standing stranglehold.
events.revealBlurb: November 10, 2020 — Apple M1. The chip integrated CPU, GPU, and memory into a single package. It was the first mainstream consumer computer to use ARM rather than x86 since the 1990s. The Mac Pro completed the Intel-to-Apple Silicon transition in 2023.

events.title: Army-McCarthy Hearings
events.blurb: A televised congressional inquiry pit a grandstanding senator against the U.S. Army, which he had accused of harboring subversives. Over 36 days, 20 million Americans watched live as his bullying tactics eroded public sympathy. The defining moment came when a quiet Boston lawyer turned to him and asked, "Have you no sense of decency, sir?"
events.revealBlurb: April 22 to June 17, 1954 — the lawyer was Joseph Welch. His line came on June 9, after McCarthy attacked a young associate. Six months later the Senate voted 67-22 to censure McCarthy. He drank himself to death within three years.

events.title: Hungarian Revolution
events.blurb: A student demonstration in Budapest grew within hours into a nationwide uprising against a Moscow-backed government. For twelve days, a reform-minded premier announced democratic elections and withdrawal from the eastern bloc military alliance. Then 2,500 Soviet tanks rolled into the country, crushing the revolt and killing some 2,500 Hungarians.
events.revealBlurb: October 23 to November 10, 1956 — reform premier Imre Nagy was tricked into a "negotiation," arrested, and secretly executed two years later. 200,000 Hungarians fled west. The West's failure to intervene exposed the limits of containment.

events.title: Berlin Wall Construction Begins
events.blurb: East German soldiers and workers erected barbed-wire barricades along the full length of the border between East and West Berlin overnight, sealing the most visible escape route from the Eastern Bloc without advance public announcement. Within days, temporary barriers were replaced with concrete, dividing families who had crossed freely just the day before.

events.title: Prague Spring Invasion
events.blurb: Reform-minded leaders in a central European capital had spent eight months experimenting with "socialism with a human face" — easing censorship, rehabilitating purge victims, and tolerating debate. In the night, 250,000 Warsaw Pact soldiers and 2,000 tanks rolled across the borders. Unarmed civilians tried to argue with the invading soldiers; within days the reforms were reversed.
events.revealBlurb: August 20-21, 1968 — invasion of Czechoslovakia. Reformist leader Alexander Dubček was flown to Moscow and forced to sign a capitulation. A student named Jan Palach set himself on fire in Wenceslas Square five months later in protest.

events.title: Berlin Wall Falls
events.blurb: An East German government spokesman announced at a press conference that citizens could cross the border immediately, triggering jubilant crowds who arrived at checkpoints and began dismantling the 155-kilometre concrete barrier with hammers and their bare hands. More than two million East Germans crossed into West Berlin during the following weekend alone.

events.title: Quit India Movement
events.blurb: After the failure of a British mission that offered only a vague promise of post-war dominion status, the Congress party launched a mass movement demanding immediate British withdrawal. The entire leadership was arrested at dawn the following day. The movement went underground and continued for years — sabotage, strikes, alternative governments in remote districts. It was violently suppressed, but British rule was visibly over as a legitimate proposition.
events.revealBlurb: August 8, 1942 — Gandhi's "Do or Die" speech at the Bombay Congress session. Churchill imprisoned 100,000 activists and held the line; by VJ Day in 1945, however, Britain was bankrupt and the political capital to hold India was gone.

events.title: Indian Independence & Partition
events.blurb: At the stroke of midnight, two new independent dominions came into existence on the subcontinent — one majority-Hindu, one majority-Muslim — as the British flag was lowered on the largest and oldest of Britain's imperial possessions. The division of provinces along religious lines displaced between 10 and 20 million people, and perhaps a million died in the communal violence that followed.
events.revealBlurb: August 14-15, 1947 — Pakistan on the 14th, India on the 15th. The boundary lines had been drawn by a London barrister, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited the subcontinent and had 36 days to complete the task. Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech was delivered at midnight from the Constituent Assembly.

events.title: Constitution of India Adopted
events.blurb: A constituent assembly of 299 members, chaired by a Bombay-trained lawyer from a once-"untouchable" community, completed two years and eleven months of debate to enact the longest written national constitution in the world — 395 articles, 22 parts, 8 schedules — establishing a secular, socialist, democratic republic. It came into force on the anniversary of a 1930 declaration of complete independence.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 1950 — B.R. Ambedkar, chair of the drafting committee. The date — Republic Day — was chosen because it marked the 20th anniversary of Congress's Purna Swaraj declaration. The final handwritten copy is illuminated by the artist Nandalal Bose.

events.title: Tashkent Declaration
events.blurb: After Soviet-mediated talks, the prime ministers of India and Pakistan signed a declaration in a Central Asian Soviet capital to end hostilities and return to the pre-war ceasefire line. The Indian prime minister died of a heart attack in his hotel room the same night, hours after signing. Conspiracy theories about his death have proliferated for decades; no autopsy was performed.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 1966 — Lal Bahadur Shastri signs, dies in Tashkent. Ayub Khan signed for Pakistan. Indira Gandhi, Nehru's daughter, succeeded Shastri as prime minister within days. Declassified files have never conclusively explained the death.

events.title: Bangladesh Liberation War
events.blurb: Pakistan's army launched a crackdown on the Bengali-speaking eastern wing of its own country, displacing an estimated 10 million refugees across the border into India. India intervened militarily; within thirteen days it had driven the Pakistani army to capitulate in a Bengali capital, where 93,000 surrendered in the largest military surrender since WWII. A new nation was born.
events.revealBlurb: December 3-16, 1971 — victory at the Instrument of Surrender at Ramna Race Course, Dhaka. Bangladesh Liberation Day is December 16. Field Marshal Sam Manekshaw commanded the Indian effort; Lt. General A.A.K. Niazi signed the surrender.

events.title: Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake Premieres
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Russian composer's first full-length ballet score premiered at a grand theatre in the Russian capital, paired with choreography that was widely thought incompetent and dancing that was widely thought under-rehearsed. Critics focused their complaints on the music, which they found too "symphonic" for dancing. Only after the composer's death, in a restaged 1895 version with new choreography, did the ballet become a classic.
events.revealBlurb: March 4, 1877 — Pyotr Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake at the Bolshoi, Moscow (Old Style February 20). The 1895 St. Petersburg revival with Petipa/Ivanov choreography is the version most companies perform today. The tragic black-swan finale was a 1950s restoration.

events.title: Elvis Records "That's All Right"
events.blurb: During a break in a fruitless recording session in Memphis, a 19-year-old truck driver began playing an uptempo blues song with such energy that the studio owner halted the session, rewound the tape, and asked him to do it again from the start. The recording blended country and rhythm-and-blues in a style that had no existing commercial category.

events.title: Woodstock Festival
events.blurb: A three-day music festival, overcapacity within hours of opening, drew an estimated 400,000 young people to a dairy farm in upstate New York despite severe rain. Fences collapsed; the event became de facto free. 32 acts performed — Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, The Who, Santana, Creedence Clearwater Revival, Joan Baez. Two people died (one from an overdose, one crushed by a tractor); two babies were born. The festival became the defining symbol of the 1960s counterculture.
events.revealBlurb: August 15-18, 1969 — on Max Yasgur's farm in Bethel, NY. Hendrix closed at 9 AM Monday morning to a dwindling crowd with a distorted, feedback-laced "Star-Spangled Banner." The 1970 documentary won an Oscar.

events.title: Elvis Presley Dies
events.blurb: A 42-year-old singer was found unresponsive on a bathroom floor of his Memphis mansion in the early afternoon and pronounced dead at a local hospital an hour later. The cause was heart failure, probably exacerbated by a cocktail of barbiturates prescribed by his personal physician. 80,000 mourners lined the four-kilometre route to the cemetery; his face had appeared on 150 magazine covers in his lifetime and would appear on tens of thousands more after his death.
events.revealBlurb: August 16, 1977 — Elvis Presley at Graceland, Memphis. An autopsy found 14 different drugs in his system. His doctor, George Nichopoulos, had his license revoked years later. "Elvis sightings" began the day after the funeral and have never entirely stopped.

events.title: Spotify Launches
events.blurb: A Swedish music-streaming service, developed in Stockholm and Stockholm alone for two years, launched invitation-only to users in six European countries. The service offered an enormous music library — eventually over 100 million tracks — free with ads or $10/month without. It would restructure the entire music business: album sales collapsed, streaming became the default, and royalties flowed through aggregation models that artists found miserly.
events.revealBlurb: October 7, 2008 — founded by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon. The service arrived in the U.S. in July 2011 after lengthy negotiations with major labels. It had 620 million monthly active users as of 2024 — the largest audio subscription service ever.

events.title: First Tour de France
events.blurb: A French sports newspaper, in an effort to increase circulation, organized a 2,428-kilometre bicycle race around the perimeter of France — six stages, each the length of an ultra-endurance event today, with sleep-deprived cyclists riding through the night on dirt roads with a single fixed gear. Sixty cyclists started; only 21 finished. A chimney sweep named Maurice Garin won the inaugural race over 19 days of riding.
events.revealBlurb: July 1-19, 1903 — organized by L'Auto magazine, a forerunner of L'Équipe. Garin's margin of victory was an implausible 2 hours 49 minutes. He was later stripped of his 1904 title for cheating (taking trains). The race continues annually with a couple of wartime interruptions.

events.title: Hank Aaron Breaks Ruth's Record
events.blurb: A 40-year-old Atlanta outfielder hit his 715th career home run off a Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher, breaking Babe Ruth's 39-year-old career record in front of a sellout home crowd. He had endured a year of death threats, racist mail, and FBI protection as he approached the record. As he rounded second base, two white college students ran onto the field alongside him — security later decided they had meant only to escort him. He tipped his cap as he crossed home plate.
events.revealBlurb: April 8, 1974 — Hank Aaron at Atlanta-Fulton County Stadium, off Al Downing. His final career total was 755 home runs, which stood as the record until Barry Bonds passed it in 2007. The FBI had warned him that multiple credible plots to assassinate him were active that season.

events.title: Phelps Wins 8 Golds in Beijing
events.blurb: A 23-year-old American swimmer won his eighth gold medal of a single Summer Olympic Games — surpassing Mark Spitz's 36-year-old record for most golds in a single Olympics. He set or broke world records in seven of the events. His final gold came in the 4x100m medley relay. Over four Olympic Games he would win a career total of 23 golds and 28 total medals, more than any athlete in any sport before him.
events.revealBlurb: August 17, 2008 — Michael Phelps at the Beijing Olympics. Spitz's previous record was 7 golds from 1972 Munich. Phelps's career gold total eventually reached 23; he retired after Rio 2016. Spitz had been a rumored spectator at many of Phelps's events.

events.title: Bolt's 9.69 100m World Record
events.blurb: A 21-year-old Jamaican sprinter won the Olympic 100-metre final in 9.69 seconds, smashing his own world record by three hundredths of a second while visibly slowing and celebrating over the final 15 metres. He ran without properly tying his shoelaces. The margin of victory over the silver medallist was the largest ever in an Olympic 100m final. Four years later in London he would set a new world record in the 200m, winning six career Olympic golds before retiring.
events.revealBlurb: August 16, 2008 — Usain Bolt at Beijing. He would drop his 100m record to 9.58 at the Berlin World Championships a year later — a mark that has never been seriously threatened. He also anchored Jamaica to world-record 4x100m relay times at three successive Olympics.

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: 19th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: Seven decades after a convention in upstate New York had narrowly resolved that women ought to vote, a Tennessee state legislator cast the deciding vote for his state's ratification — after reading a telegram from his mother urging him to do so. Women across the United States gained the national vote in time for the November presidential election, in which 8 million new voters participated.
events.revealBlurb: August 18, 1920 — the deciding vote was cast by Harry T. Burn, age 24. His mother's letter read: "Hurrah, and vote for suffrage. Don't keep them in doubt." The amendment was certified on August 26, now Women's Equality Day.

events.title: Roe v. Wade
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that the right to privacy implicit in the 14th Amendment protected a woman's decision to terminate a pregnancy, striking down most state abortion laws. The ruling established a three-trimester framework balancing state interests against individual rights. It would remain the governing precedent for 49 years, until its overturn in 2022 returned abortion regulation to the states.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1973 — plaintiff "Jane Roe" was Norma McCorvey, who never actually had the abortion. She changed her position on the issue multiple times before her death in 2017. The ruling was overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson on June 24, 2022.

events.title: Sally Ride in Space
events.blurb: A 32-year-old astrophysicist, riding as mission specialist aboard a space shuttle launched from a Florida coastal site, became the first American woman — and the youngest American — to reach orbit. NASA had asked her at the pre-flight press conference whether space travel would affect her reproductive organs; she answered that there was no evidence either way.
events.revealBlurb: June 18, 1983 — Space Shuttle Challenger, STS-7 mission. She flew a second mission in 1984 and was on the commission investigating the 1986 Challenger disaster that killed seven of her colleagues. She came out as a lesbian in her 2012 obituary.

events.title: Benazir Bhutto Becomes PM
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Oxford and Harvard educated politician whose father had been hanged by a previous military government was sworn in as prime minister of a large South Asian Muslim-majority country, becoming the first woman to head the government of any Muslim-majority state. Her ruling coalition was fragile; she would be dismissed twice on corruption charges and would be assassinated 19 years later while campaigning for a third term.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1988 — Benazir Bhutto of Pakistan. She was assassinated in Rawalpindi on December 27, 2007, after a campaign rally. Her 19-year-old son Bilawal was named co-chair of her party within days.

events.title: Ruth Bader Ginsburg Confirmed
events.blurb: A 60-year-old federal appeals court judge, a former ACLU lawyer who had successfully argued six of the era's most important gender-discrimination cases before the court she was now joining, was confirmed 96-3 as the second woman to sit on the U.S. Supreme Court. She would serve 27 years, becoming — somewhat unexpectedly for a cautious litigator — a late-life pop-culture icon on the Court's liberal wing.
events.revealBlurb: August 10, 1993 — nominated by Bill Clinton. She acquired the nickname "Notorious RBG" from a law student's Tumblr in 2013. She died September 18, 2020, enabling the confirmation of Amy Coney Barrett eight days before the presidential election.

events.title: Electromagnetic Field Equations Published
events.blurb: A Scottish physicist unified electricity, magnetism, and light into a single mathematical framework of four equations, showing that changing electric fields produce magnetic fields and vice versa — generating self-propagating waves that travel at the speed of light. The equations predicted that light was an electromagnetic wave and implied the existence of radio waves, infrared radiation, and other forms not yet observed.
events.revealBlurb: 1865 — James Clerk Maxwell's paper was read to the Royal Society in December 1864. Heinrich Hertz experimentally confirmed the existence of radio waves in 1887, nine years after Maxwell died of cancer at 48. Richard Feynman called Maxwell's equations "the most significant event of the 19th century" — a bold statement given the century's competition.

events.title: Mendel's Laws of Inheritance Published
events.blurb: After eight years of cross-breeding pea plants and counting roughly 29,000 offspring, an Austrian monk published statistical ratios showing that heritable traits are passed in discrete units — dominant and recessive — and that different traits are inherited independently of one another. The paper described the mathematical foundations of heredity without any knowledge of chromosomes or DNA.
events.revealBlurb: 1866 — the paper was presented at two meetings in 1865 and published a year later, then ignored for 34 years. When three European botanists independently rediscovered the same ratios in 1900 and searched the prior literature, they all found Mendel's paper at the same time. He had died sixteen years earlier.

events.title: Helium Detected in the Sun
events.blurb: During a total solar eclipse, a French astronomer studying the spectrum of light from the Sun's outer atmosphere found a bright yellow spectral line that matched no known element on Earth, suggesting the existence of a new element present in the Sun but not yet found on our planet. Two months later, an English astronomer independently identified the same line and gave the element its name, derived from the Greek word for the Sun.
events.revealBlurb: August 18, 1868 — Janssen realised during the eclipse that the bright chromospheric lines could be observed in daylight without an eclipse and invented the spectroscope for doing so. Helium was not detected on Earth for another 27 years, when it was found in a uranium mineral in 1895. It is the only element discovered in space before being found on Earth.

events.title: Electron Announced
events.blurb: During a lecture at a London scientific institution, a physicist announced that cathode rays were composed of particles roughly one-thousandth the mass of a hydrogen atom — the first demonstration that atoms were not the smallest units of matter. The particles were initially called "corpuscles"; the modern name came from a suggestion by an Irish physicist the same year.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1897 — J.J. Thomson's discovery won him the Nobel Prize in 1906, and his son George Thomson won a separate Nobel in 1937 for proving the electron was a wave. Father and son together proved it was a particle and a wave — one of physics' neatest family rivalries.

events.title: Plate Tectonics Theory Accepted
events.blurb: After decades of ridicule, a theory holding that Earth's crust is fractured into massive slabs drifting centimetres each year was vindicated by magnetic stripe patterns mapped on either side of mid-ocean ridges. The pattern matched predictions for seafloor spreading, explaining continental shapes, mountain ranges, and earthquake zones in a single framework.
events.revealBlurb: 1967–68 — the "plate tectonics revolution". Alfred Wegener had proposed continental drift in 1912 and been mocked for it; he died in 1930 on an expedition in Greenland. Geologists officially accepted his core idea thirty-seven years after his death.

events.title: A Trip to the Moon Released
events.blurb: A former stage magician released a 14-minute narrative film depicting a group of astronomers launched to the Moon in a giant bullet fired from a cannon, encountering hostile selenites, and returning to Earth. Its hand-tinted prints included the most recognizable image in early cinema: a cartoon Moon with a bullet lodged in its eye. It was pirated within months by Thomas Edison's company, which sold copies without paying royalties.
events.revealBlurb: 1902 — Georges Méliès, whose production company Star Film went bankrupt partly from lost piracy revenue. He destroyed many of his own negatives in bitterness; the hand-coloured version was rediscovered in Barcelona in 1993, disintegrating, and painstakingly restored.

events.title: The Jazz Singer Released
events.blurb: A Warner Brothers feature film about a cantor's son who runs away to become a vaudeville singer premiered at a Times Square theatre as the first full-length motion picture with synchronized recorded dialogue. The star, in blackface for most of the film, delivered the industry's first-ever spoken movie line: "Wait a minute, wait a minute. You ain't heard nothin' yet!" Within three years almost every Hollywood film was a talkie.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 1927 — Al Jolson at the Warners' Theatre, NYC. The film's sound system, Vitaphone, used synchronized phonograph records rather than optical audio. The silent era ended astonishingly fast; by 1930 the major Hollywood studios had written off the previous decade's technology.

events.title: Rashomon Released
events.blurb: A 40-year-old Japanese director released a 88-minute film in which the same violent encounter is recounted by four different participants, none of whom agrees with any of the others. The Venice Film Festival awarded it the Golden Lion the following year, and the world film industry discovered Japanese cinema as a major force. The very title became an English noun: "the Rashomon effect" is the concept of contradictory memories.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1950 — Akira Kurosawa. The producers were reportedly baffled by the script and wanted it re-edited. Its Venice win completely blindsided Japanese critics, who had not thought much of the film. It led directly to the global reception of Ozu, Mizoguchi, and Kurosawa's later work.

events.title: Pather Panchali Released
events.blurb: A first-time director shot a Bengali village drama across three years in fragments whenever he could afford to — including pawning his wife's jewellery to finish an opening sequence of a boy chasing a train through tall grass. It won a Humanist Prize at Cannes and launched a tradition of realist Indian cinema that bypassed Bombay entirely.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1955 — Satyajit Ray's debut. He was a commercial illustrator with no directing experience; the crew were mostly amateurs. The score was composed by an then-obscure sitarist named Ravi Shankar, recorded in a single 11-hour session. The West Bengal government funded its completion after seeing rough footage.

events.title: Star Wars Released
events.blurb: A 33-year-old American director released a science-fiction film mashing up elements of samurai cinema, WWII dogfight pictures, and Joseph Campbell's monomyth theory, with groundbreaking effects assembled in a repurposed warehouse with a workforce assembled from scratch. The studio had cut his budget and expected the film to flop; one executive had retitled it "The Adventures of Luke Starkiller." Lines began forming at theatres on opening morning and did not stop for years.
events.revealBlurb: May 25, 1977 — George Lucas. He traded his directing salary for merchandising rights; he became a billionaire. The effects company he had to build from scratch, Industrial Light & Magic, became the industry standard for decades. Campbell wept watching the film.

events.title: Dante Completes Divine Comedy
events.blurb: A 56-year-old exiled Florentine poet completed the third and final part of a long allegorical poem describing his journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Heaven, guided by a Roman poet and his earthly beloved. Written in Italian rather than Latin, it pulled the vernacular into literary respectability. He died within months of finishing.
events.revealBlurb: 1320 — Dante Alighieri. He had been exiled from Florence in 1302 over factional politics; he never returned. The last 13 cantos of Paradiso were missing for months after his death until his son Jacopo found them in a secret cavity in a wall, supposedly after Dante appeared in a dream.

events.title: Paradise Lost Published
events.blurb: A blind 58-year-old English poet, dictating to a rotating cast of scribes, completed a 10-book (later 12-book) epic poem retelling the Biblical account of the fall of man from the perspective of a sympathetically characterized Satan. Having narrowly escaped execution for his political writings under the restored monarchy, he was paid ten pounds for the manuscript. It would become the template for English epic poetry.
events.revealBlurb: 1667 — John Milton. He had gone blind in 1652 from untreated glaucoma. His daughters had to be taught to read — including Hebrew, Greek, and Latin — just so they could transcribe his dictations. "The mind is its own place..." is from Book I.

events.title: Johnson's Dictionary Published
events.blurb: An Oxford-educated English essayist, working nine years with six assistants in a garret flat, completed and published a two-volume dictionary of the English language — the first comprehensive, systematically illustrated dictionary of the vernacular. It defined 42,773 words with 114,000 quotations showing their use. It was the standard English dictionary until Oxford's larger project finally superseded it 173 years later.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1755 — Samuel Johnson. He defined "lexicographer" as "a harmless drudge, that busies himself in tracing the original, and detailing the signification of words." His tart definitions became famous in their own right: "Oats: A grain, which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people."

events.title: War and Peace Published
events.blurb: A 41-year-old Russian aristocrat completed the last serial installment of a vast historical novel following five aristocratic families through Russia's Napoleonic Wars. The finished work ran over 1,200 pages and combined personal drama, military history, and a 200-page essay on the philosophy of history tacked onto the end. The author rewrote the opening sentence at least seven times.
events.revealBlurb: 1869 — Leo Tolstoy. It was serialized in the journal Russky Vestnik between 1865 and 1869. Tolstoy later disowned most of his fiction on religious grounds and decades later attempted to destroy his own estate's copyright to prevent his heirs from profiting.

events.title: Harry Potter First Book Published
events.blurb: A 32-year-old single mother who had drafted most of the manuscript in Edinburgh cafés over six years, on single-parent benefits, published her first novel after twelve rejections from other publishers. The first print run was 500 copies; 300 went to libraries. Children started reading, telling friends, and returning. Within four years the series had become the most successful in publishing history; she would become the first novelist to reach a billion-dollar net worth.
events.revealBlurb: June 26, 1997 — J.K. Rowling, "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (US title: "Sorcerer's Stone"). Her publisher Bloomsbury suggested using "J.K." instead of Joanne because boys might not read a book by a woman. The series has sold over 600 million copies.

events.title: 14th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: Ratified in the aftermath of civil war, a constitutional amendment granted citizenship to "all persons born or naturalized in the United States," promised them equal protection under the laws, and guaranteed due process. Its sweeping language became, a century later, the foundation of Supreme Court rulings on school segregation, interracial marriage, abortion, and marriage equality.
events.revealBlurb: July 9, 1868 — citizenship via birthright. Its authors were thinking of formerly enslaved people; its practical effect reshaped virtually every area of American law. The "equal protection clause" alone has been cited in over 400 Supreme Court cases.

events.title: Executive Order 8802
events.blurb: Facing a threatened mass march on Washington organized by a prominent Black labor leader, a U.S. president signed an executive order banning racial discrimination in the defense industry and federal government. It was the first federal action against employment discrimination since Reconstruction. The threatened march was called off; the larger March would come 22 years later.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1941 — Franklin Roosevelt, pushed by A. Philip Randolph. Randolph had assembled 100,000 marchers and refused to call it off without the order. The order created the Fair Employment Practice Committee — a template for later civil rights enforcement.

events.title: Emmett Till Murdered
events.blurb: A 14-year-old Black boy visiting family in a rural Southern state was abducted from his great-uncle's home in the middle of the night, tortured, shot, and thrown into a river with a cotton-gin fan tied around his neck. His mother insisted on an open-casket funeral so the world could see what had been done to her son. Photographs of the mutilated body, published in Jet magazine, galvanized a generation.
events.revealBlurb: August 28, 1955 — Money, Mississippi. His accuser, Carolyn Bryant, admitted decades later she had lied about the encounter. Her husband and his half-brother were acquitted by an all-white jury, then sold their confession to Look magazine knowing they couldn't be retried.

events.title: Birmingham Children's Crusade
events.blurb: Over several days in a notoriously segregated Alabama steel city, more than a thousand Black schoolchildren — some as young as 6 — marched out of classes in organized protest. Police commissioner Bull Connor ordered fire hoses and attack dogs deployed against them. Photographs of a teenage boy lunged at by a German shepherd appeared on front pages across the world.
events.revealBlurb: May 2-5, 1963 — Birmingham, Alabama. King agreed to use children over the objections of many advisers; they were less vulnerable to losing jobs for protesting. Within weeks, the Kennedy administration introduced what became the Civil Rights Act.

events.title: March on Washington
events.blurb: A quarter-million Americans — three-quarters Black, a quarter white — gathered between the Washington and Lincoln Memorials on the 100th anniversary summer of the Emancipation Proclamation to demand the passage of civil-rights legislation then stalled in Congress. The event's closing address, given on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, contained a phrase repeated in eight paragraphs: "I have a dream."
events.revealBlurb: August 28, 1963. MLK's prepared text did not contain "I have a dream" — Mahalia Jackson, behind him on the dais, shouted "Tell them about the dream, Martin!" and he ad-libbed the most famous passage. The Justice Department had 4,000 troops on standby in case of violence. None was needed.

events.title: U.S. Constitution Signed
events.blurb: Fifty-five delegates meeting for four months in a Philadelphia state house, working in secret through a sweltering summer with the windows closed against spies, produced a seven-article document replacing the loose Articles of Confederation with a stronger federal framework. Thirty-nine of them signed. An 81-year-old Benjamin Franklin, who had been at nearly every session, pointed at the sun carved into George Washington's chair and said he was finally sure it was rising, not setting.
events.revealBlurb: September 17, 1787 — Independence Hall, Philadelphia. Ratified June 21, 1788 after New Hampshire became the ninth state to approve. The Constitution has been amended 27 times in 235 years — less than once per decade. A different Philadelphia-era document, the Bill of Rights, followed in 1791.

events.title: Declaration of the Rights of Man
events.blurb: The French National Constituent Assembly, meeting in a recently converted royal indoor tennis court, adopted a 17-article statement of universal rights: liberty, property, security, resistance to oppression, equality before the law, presumption of innocence, freedom of speech and religion.
