It did not grant women the vote or abolish slavery; revolutionaries would debate those extensions for years. It was still the most sweeping such declaration any European state had ever adopted.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1789 — a central drafter was the Marquis de Lafayette, the American Revolution veteran. The declaration was explicitly modeled on the U.S. Declaration of Independence; in fact, Jefferson, then in Paris as American minister, advised on its drafting. It remains part of France's constitutional law.

events.title: Haitian Revolution Begins
events.blurb: A voodoo ceremony in a wooded area of a French Caribbean sugar colony marked the coordinated signal for a mass uprising of enslaved Africans. Within ten days, plantations across the northern plain were in flames and 4,000 whites and mulattos were dead. It was the largest slave revolt in the history of the Americas and the only one that successfully established an independent state. The colony had been the richest in the Western hemisphere; it produced 40 percent of the world's sugar.
events.revealBlurb: August 22, 1791 — Saint-Domingue (now Haiti). The ceremony was at Bois Caïman, led by voodoo priest Dutty Boukman. Toussaint Louverture emerged as principal leader, though he was captured by the French in 1802 and died in a freezing French prison cell. Independence came on January 1, 1804.

events.title: Napoleon Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Corsican-born general, having ruled France as First Consul for five years, staged a coronation at the Gothic cathedral in the French capital. He had negotiated the pope's attendance; in the ceremony's most famous moment — possibly prearranged, possibly improvised — the emperor took the crown from the pope and placed it on his own head. The act was read as a message: no religious authority ratified his power.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1804 — Notre-Dame de Paris. Pope Pius VII had been brought from Rome; he sat largely passive through the ceremony. Napoleon's wife Joséphine also crowned herself empress. Jacques-Louis David's monumental painting of the coronation, finished three years later, flatters Napoleon's height among other details.

events.title: Battle of Austerlitz
events.blurb: A French army of 68,000 men, outnumbered by a combined Russian and Austrian force of 89,000, achieved what is still regarded as one of the greatest tactical victories in military history. Feigning weakness, the French commander baited his opponents into attacking his deliberately weakened right flank, then counter-attacked through the centre as the enemy's lines stretched thin. Three emperors had taken the field; two retreated; the Holy Roman Empire would formally dissolve within a year.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1805 — Napoleon's victory over Tsar Alexander I and Emperor Francis II, on the first anniversary of his coronation. The battle is also called "the Battle of the Three Emperors." Allied casualties: ~36,000. French: ~9,000.

events.title: Sputnik 1 Orbital Launch
events.blurb: A polished aluminum sphere the size of a beach ball lifted off from a steppe launch site and became the first human-made object to orbit Earth. Weighing 83 kilograms and trailing four whip antennas, it circled the planet every 96 minutes and broadcast a radio beep on 20 and 40 MHz audible to amateur operators worldwide for 22 days until its batteries died.
events.revealBlurb: October 4, 1957 — Sputnik 1. It carried zero scientific instruments; the entire payload was a thermometer and a radio transmitter. The beep's rhythm changed with cabin temperature, which meant the world's most-tracked signal was also the world's first space weather report.

events.title: First Woman in Space
events.blurb: Valentina Tereshkova, a 26-year-old former textile factory worker and amateur parachutist with no pilot training, launched aboard Vostok 6 and orbited Earth 48 times over nearly three days — more total time in space than all US astronauts who had flown to that date combined. She performed observations and photographed aerosol layers in Earth's atmosphere before parachuting to a landing in Kazakhstan.
events.revealBlurb: June 16, 1963 — Vostok 6. Tereshkova selected herself from 400 applicants by writing a letter directly to the Soviet Space Program. She reportedly got motion sick and did not conduct some planned manual maneuvers, a fact kept classified for years. No woman flew in space again for 19 years. She remains the only woman to have flown a solo space mission.

events.title: Mir Space Station Deorbit
events.blurb: Russia deliberately deorbited the Mir space station after 15 years of continuous operation, using three burns from a docked Progress cargo spacecraft to lower its orbit until it reentered the atmosphere over the South Pacific. Most of the station burned up during reentry, but approximately 1,500 kg of debris survived and splashed into the ocean between Australia and Chile.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2001 — Mir deorbit. Mir had been in orbit so long that cosmonauts reported the walls were alive with mold. A Russian company sold pay-per-view rights to watch the reentry from a chartered aircraft. Japan offered to purchase and keep the station operational; the deal fell through over cost. It had been visited by 104 cosmonauts and astronauts from 12 nations.

events.title: James Webb Space Telescope Launch
events.blurb: An Ariane 5 rocket launched the James Webb Space Telescope from Kourou, French Guiana, sending the largest and most complex space observatory ever built toward the second Lagrange point 1.5 million km from Earth. The 6.5-meter gold-coated beryllium mirror — too large to fit in the rocket fairing — had to fold origami-style and then unfurl over two weeks after launch.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 2021 — JWST. The telescope took 30 years and approximately $10 billion to build, surviving 17 major redesigns and two near-cancellations by Congress. Because the rocket had such a precise trajectory, JWST arrived at L2 with enough fuel margin to operate for 20 years instead of the planned 10. Its first image release on July 12, 2022 showed 13.1-billion-year-old light.

events.title: First South Pole Moon Landing
events.blurb: India's Chandrayaan-3 Vikram lander set down at 69°S latitude near the lunar south pole — the highest-latitude soft landing on the Moon ever achieved — just days after a Russian Luna-25 mission attempting the same target crashed on approach. The Pragyan rover confirmed the presence of sulfur, oxygen, iron, and other elements in the regolith through laser spectroscopy.
events.revealBlurb: August 23, 2023 — Chandrayaan-3. The mission cost approximately $75 million — cheaper than many Hollywood blockbusters and a fraction of comparable NASA missions. India became only the fourth nation to soft-land on the Moon and the first to reach the south polar region. The rover covered 100 meters before being placed in sleep mode ahead of the lunar night; it did not wake up.

events.title: Eruption of Vesuvius
events.blurb: A volcano on the Italian peninsula, dormant for centuries and believed extinct by the farmers whose vineyards clung to its slopes, erupted in a single day, burying two wealthy resort towns and their roughly 16,000 inhabitants under 6 metres of ash, pumice, and pyroclastic flow. The buried cities lay undiscovered for 1,700 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 79 CE — Pompeii and Herculaneum, under Mount Vesuvius. Pliny the Younger watched from across the Bay of Naples and wrote the only eyewitness account. Volcanologists still classify massive plinian eruptions by his name.

events.title: Spanish Flu Pandemic Begins
events.blurb: An unusually lethal strain of influenza, carried through military camps and troop ships during the final months of a world war, infected a third of the planet and killed an estimated 50 to 100 million people in three successive waves over two years. Unlike most flus, it disproportionately killed healthy young adults by triggering cytokine storms in robust immune systems.
events.revealBlurb: March 1918 — first identified at a US Army base in Kansas. It was called "Spanish" only because wartime censorship in belligerent countries suppressed coverage; neutral Spain reported it freely, so it seemed to originate there. It had nothing to do with Spain.

events.title: European Heat Wave
events.blurb: A prolonged period of extreme heat, with temperatures over 40°C across much of western Europe, killed an estimated 70,000 people, mostly elderly apartment-dwellers in cities poorly equipped for such conditions. France alone lost 15,000 lives. Morgues ran out of space; refrigerated trucks were requisitioned.
events.revealBlurb: August 2003 — France, Italy, Spain, UK, and Germany hit hardest. Paris reached 40°C. Many elderly victims were discovered by returning holidaymakers weeks later. France rewrote its social services to check on isolated seniors; subsequent heat waves in 2006, 2019, and 2022 killed far fewer.

events.title: Hurricane Katrina
events.blurb: A Category 3 hurricane made landfall on the US Gulf Coast, driving a storm surge that overtopped and breached the levee system protecting a major port city lying largely below sea level. 80 percent of the city flooded; 1,392 people died. The chaotic federal response — images of thousands stranded on a sports stadium roof, bodies floating in water — inflicted lasting damage on the administration in power.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 2005 — New Orleans, Louisiana. The Superdome housed 30,000 evacuees for five days in deteriorating conditions. The head of FEMA, Michael Brown, had previously run the International Arabian Horse Association; he resigned within two weeks.

events.title: Maui Wildfires
events.blurb: High winds from a distant hurricane drove grass fires through a historic town on a Hawaiian island, reaching speeds that outpaced emergency alerts. 102 people died — many trapped in cars attempting to flee along a single coastal road — in the deadliest US wildfire in over a century. The 19th-century whaling-era town of Lāhainā, once the kingdom capital, was almost completely destroyed.
events.revealBlurb: August 8, 2023 — Lāhainā, Maui. The outdoor warning siren network, the largest in the world, was never activated. Some survivors escaped by jumping into the Pacific Ocean and treading water for hours. Downed Hawaiian Electric lines were identified as the likely ignition source.

events.title: Invasion of Poland
events.blurb: At 4:43 in the morning a warship opened fire on a peninsula garrison, and within minutes armoured columns and aircraft were crossing a national border along a 1,600-kilometre front from three directions simultaneously. Two days later, two of the invader's neighbours declared war — and the world's largest conflict had begun.
events.revealBlurb: September 1, 1939 — the battleship Schleswig-Holstein fired the first shots at Westerplatte. The 88-man garrison held out for seven days against a force many times its size. Poland was split between Germany and the Soviet Union by October 6; a government-in-exile continued the fight from London.

events.title: Scuttling of the Graf Spee
events.blurb: A feared commerce-raider that had sunk nine merchant ships in three months limped into a neutral harbour for repairs after a running battle with three smaller cruisers, then sat immobile while international diplomacy set a 72-hour countdown. Twenty thousand spectators lined the waterfront to watch her captain make his final decision.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1939, Montevideo. Captain Hans Langsdorff scuttled the Admiral Graf Spee at 8:55 PM rather than risk his crew in what he believed was an overwhelming British trap. Three days later he wrapped himself in the ship's battle ensign and shot himself. The trap was largely bluff.

events.title: Tehran Conference
events.blurb: The three most powerful leaders of the opposing alliance met for the first time in a capital city in southwest Asia, committing to a firm timeline for a massive cross-channel invasion in spring, agreeing on the postwar borders of one eastern European nation, and beginning to sketch the political shape of the world that would follow the conflict.
events.revealBlurb: November 28 – December 1, 1943 — FDR, Churchill, and Stalin met in Tehran. It was the first time FDR and Stalin met in person. Roosevelt, whose security staff feared assassination, moved into the Soviet Embassy at Stalin's suggestion — and Soviet intelligence promptly bugged his suite. Churchill celebrated his 69th birthday at the conference with a dinner attended by all three leaders.

events.title: Liberation of Paris
events.blurb: A city that had been under foreign occupation for four years erupted into street fighting as its own police force led an uprising, then fell into celebration as armoured columns rolled through its boulevards, the military governor surrendered, and a tall general delivered an emotional speech from the steps of a historic civic building to a vast and weeping crowd.
events.revealBlurb: August 25, 1944. German General Dietrich von Choltitz surrendered despite Hitler's repeated orders to destroy the city's bridges, monuments, and water system. Von Choltitz later claimed he had ignored the orders to preserve Paris; historians note he may simply have lacked the engineers and explosives. De Gaulle's famous speech began: "Paris! Paris outraged! Paris broken! Paris martyred! But Paris liberated!"

events.title: Execution of Mussolini
events.blurb: The founder of one of the 20th century's major fascist movements was captured hiding in a German military convoy while attempting to flee across a northern border, taken to a lakeside village by communist partisans, and shot 26 hours later — his body then transported to a major city and hung upside down at a petrol station for public display.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 1945 — executed at Giulino di Mezzegra on Lake Como, two days before Hitler's death. Mussolini and his mistress Clara Petacci were shot, then driven to Milan and strung up by their heels at the Piazzale Loreto — the same square where partisan hostages had been publicly displayed by Fascists a year earlier.

events.title: U.S. Constitution Ratified
events.blurb: New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify the proposed Constitution, providing the three-fourths supermajority required to bring the new framework of government into effect and replace the faltering Articles of Confederation. The document created a federal republic with three separated branches of power — a design that had no exact precedent in world history.
events.revealBlurb: June 21, 1788 — New Hampshire. Rhode Island didn't ratify until May 1790 — over a year after the government had already begun operating. North Carolina waited until November 1789, after the First Congress had already convened.

events.title: Battle of New Orleans
events.blurb: General Andrew Jackson's patchwork army of Tennessee frontiersmen, Louisiana militia, free Black soldiers, Choctaw warriors, and pirates under Jean Lafitte decisively routed an 8,000-strong British force attempting to seize New Orleans, killing or wounding roughly 2,000 redcoats while suffering fewer than 70 American casualties. The lopsided victory made Jackson a national hero and propelled him to the presidency.
events.revealBlurb: January 8, 1815 — Chalmette, Louisiana. The Treaty of Ghent ending the War of 1812 had been signed 15 days earlier — news hadn't arrived. The battle had zero effect on the war's official outcome but enormous effect on American mythology and Jackson's political career.

events.title: Women's Suffrage Amendment Certified
events.blurb: The U.S. Secretary of State certified the ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment, prohibiting any state from denying the right to vote on account of sex. The amendment's passage followed a 72-year organised campaign that had begun at the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848, when most of its original signatories were ridiculed for the demand.

events.title: Taft-Hartley Act Becomes Law
events.blurb: The Republican-controlled 80th Congress overrode President Harry Truman's veto, enacting the Labor-Management Relations Act — known as Taft-Hartley — which restricted union activities, banned secondary boycotts and solidarity strikes, permitted states to pass right-to-work laws, and required union officers to swear they were not Communists. The law fundamentally reshaped the relationship between organized labor and the federal government.
events.revealBlurb: June 23, 1947 — Washington, D.C. Truman called it a "slave labor bill" in his veto message, though he later used its provisions himself to break the 1952 steel strike. Union membership peaked at about 35% of the workforce in the late 1940s; by 2024 it had fallen to roughly 10%.

events.title: Watergate Break-In
events.blurb: At 2:30 in the morning, Washington D.C. police arrested five men inside the headquarters of the Democratic National Committee at the Watergate complex, where they had broken in to photograph documents and plant surveillance devices. The burglars were connected to the Committee to Re-Elect the President, and the discovery of the break-in and the subsequent cover-up by the Nixon White House eventually destroyed his presidency.
events.revealBlurb: June 17, 1972 — Watergate complex, Washington, D.C. The burglars were caught because a security guard noticed tape on a door latch and called the police. Nixon won re-election in November 1972 in one of the largest landslides in American history — 520 to 17 electoral votes — while the cover-up was already underway.

events.title: Great Fire of London
events.blurb: A blaze beginning in a baker's shop on Pudding Lane burned for four days, destroying 373 acres of the medieval city including 13,200 houses, 87 churches, and most civic buildings. The fire melted the lead roof of St. Paul's Cathedral and was visible 60 miles away, yet officially killed only six people due to rapid evacuation before the flames spread.

events.title: Krakatoa Eruption
events.blurb: An island volcano in the strait between two large Indonesian islands exploded in a series of detonations culminating in a final blast so loud it was heard 4,800 kilometres away and circled the planet four times as a pressure wave. The eruption generated tsunamis that killed 36,000 people on surrounding coasts; the resulting atmospheric dust produced red-green sunsets worldwide for years.
events.revealBlurb: August 27, 1883 — Krakatoa, Sunda Strait. The final explosion had an acoustic energy roughly equivalent to 200 megatons of TNT. The glow of the afterburn may be what Edvard Munch painted in The Scream a decade later.

events.title: Mount Pelée Eruption
events.blurb: A volcanic mountain on a Caribbean island unleashed a pyroclastic flow — a superheated cloud of gas and ash travelling at hurricane speed — that swept down onto the colonial capital below and killed nearly every one of the town's 28,000 inhabitants in about 60 seconds. Two survivors were found: a shoemaker on the outskirts and a prisoner locked in a thick-walled dungeon.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1902 — Saint-Pierre, Martinique. The prisoner, Ludger Sylbaris, was saved by his stone cell, horribly burned but alive. He later joined Barnum & Bailey Circus as "the man who lived through Doomsday."

events.title: Tunguska Event
events.blurb: A massive explosion in the atmosphere above a remote Siberian forest flattened some 80 million trees over an area of 2,150 square kilometres. Eyewitnesses 60 kilometres away were thrown from their chairs. Seismic stations across Europe registered the blast. The first scientific expedition did not reach the site for 19 years. No impact crater was ever found.
events.revealBlurb: June 30, 1908 — Tunguska, Russian Empire. Current consensus: a stony asteroid 50-60 metres across exploded about 8 kilometres up. If it had arrived five hours later, it would have hit St. Petersburg. The date is now International Asteroid Day.

events.title: Tōhoku Earthquake & Fukushima
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the Pacific coast of northern Japan triggered tsunami waves up to 40 metres high that killed some 19,700 people and swamped the seawalls of a coastal nuclear plant. Three reactor cores melted down in the following days, contaminating 337 square kilometres of surrounding countryside. 165,000 people were displaced; many never returned.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 2011 — 2:46 PM local time. The quake was so powerful it shifted Earth's axis by about 17 centimetres and shortened the day by 1.8 microseconds. The plant's operator, TEPCO, had been warned about tsunami risk years earlier and ignored it.

events.title: Battle of Actium
events.blurb: Off the coast of northwestern Greece, Octavian's fleet under Marcus Agrippa met the combined ships of Mark Antony and Cleopatra. When Cleopatra's Egyptian squadron broke off and fled mid-battle, Antony abandoned his own fleet to follow her; his 19 legions on shore surrendered a week later. The last serious rival to a single ruler of Rome was gone.
events.revealBlurb: September 2, 31 BCE. Antony and Cleopatra escaped to Alexandria, where both committed suicide the following year — Antony by falling on his sword (badly), Cleopatra by asp bite (legend) or poison. Octavian kept Cleopatra's son Caesarion alive just long enough to read Caesar's will, then had him killed.

events.title: Diocletian's Tetrarchy
events.blurb: Recognising that one man could not govern and defend an empire stretching from Scotland to Mesopotamia, Emperor Diocletian formalised a system of four co-rulers — two senior Augusti and two junior Caesars — each commanding a quarter of the empire from a frontier capital. He also doubled the size of the army, reformed the tax system, and set maximum prices for hundreds of goods.
events.revealBlurb: 293 CE. Diocletian is the only Roman emperor to voluntarily abdicate and retire — he went to grow cabbages in his palace at Split (modern Croatia). When colleagues urged him to return, he reportedly replied that if they could see the cabbages he had grown, they would not ask.

events.title: Julian the Apostate's Pagan Revival
events.blurb: Emperor Julian — Constantine's nephew, raised as a Christian — publicly renounced Christianity upon taking power, reopened pagan temples that had been confiscated or closed, restored their revenues, and barred Christians from teaching classical literature in schools. He lasted only eighteen months before dying from a spear wound during a Persian campaign.
events.revealBlurb: November 361 CE. Julian wrote philosophical treatises, got up before dawn to perform sacrifices, and reportedly sacrificed so many oxen that soldiers nicknamed him "the Slaughterhouse." His pagan restoration died with him; every successor returned to Christianity.

events.title: Permanent Division of the Roman Empire
events.blurb: On his deathbed in Mediolanum, Emperor Theodosius divided the empire between his two sons: eighteen-year-old Arcadius took the east with Constantinople, and ten-year-old Honorius took the west with its capital at Ravenna. No mechanism existed to reunite the two halves, and none ever did.
events.revealBlurb: January 17, 395 CE. Theodosius was the last man to rule the entire Roman Empire. His ten-year-old western heir Honorius grew up to be a notably passive emperor; later historians note that when told "Rome has fallen," he reportedly burst into tears — then relaxed when he learned it was the city, not his favourite hen, also named "Rome."

events.title: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
events.blurb: The Germanic warlord Odoacer deposed the sixteen-year-old emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna — a boy whose mocking nickname meant "Little Augustus" — and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, informing the eastern emperor that the west no longer needed a separate ruler. Odoacer spared Romulus's life, finding him too young and too minor to bother executing, and exiled him to a villa in Campania on a pension.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 476 CE. The last western emperor's name combined the city's legendary founder and its first emperor — an irony Roman writers noticed immediately. Contemporaries did not regard this moment as "the fall of Rome"; that framing came centuries later. The eastern empire in Constantinople continued for another 977 years.

events.title: Great Kantō Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck the main Japanese island at noon, as hundreds of thousands of households were preparing lunch over charcoal braziers. The fires that erupted in the collapsed wooden city were fanned by a typhoon passing offshore, merging into a single firestorm with tornadoes of flame. Around 140,000 people died; 1.9 million were left homeless.
events.revealBlurb: September 1, 1923 — Tokyo and Yokohama. A persistent false rumor that ethnic Koreans were poisoning wells led to vigilante massacres of some 6,000 Korean residents. September 1 is now Japan's Disaster Prevention Day.

events.title: Hurricane Andrew
events.blurb: A compact Category 5 hurricane made landfall in southern Florida in the early hours of a late summer morning, its eyewall gusts reaching 280 km/h. It destroyed 63,500 houses, left 175,000 people homeless, and caused $27 billion in damage — then the costliest natural disaster in US history. Building codes across the Florida peninsula were rewritten as a direct consequence.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 1992 — Homestead, Florida. It was the first named storm of an otherwise quiet season. Eleven insurance companies went bankrupt settling claims. For comparison, Katrina 13 years later cost over $100 billion.

events.title: Indian Ocean Tsunami
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the western coast of Sumatra — the third-largest ever recorded — displaced so much water that tsunami waves up to 30 metres high raced across the Indian Ocean, hitting 14 countries within hours. Around 228,000 people died in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, Thailand, and as far away as Somalia. No warning system existed.
events.revealBlurb: December 26, 2004 — Boxing Day. A 10-year-old British girl named Tilly Smith recognized the receding tide from a school geography lesson and got her family's Phuket beach evacuated, saving around 100 lives. A basin-wide warning system was operational by 2006.

events.title: Deepwater Horizon Spill
events.blurb: A blowout on a semi-submersible drilling rig in the Gulf of Mexico killed 11 workers and severed the riser pipe to a well 1,500 metres below the surface. Over the next 87 days, as engineers tried increasingly improbable methods to cap it, roughly 780 million litres of crude oil gushed into the sea — the largest accidental marine oil spill in history.
events.revealBlurb: April 20, 2010 — off Louisiana. The well was finally killed in mid-September. BP paid over $65 billion in settlements, fines, and cleanup. A live-stream of the ocean-floor plume was watched by millions during the crisis; executives who claimed it was "relatively tiny" became memes.

events.title: Black Summer Bushfires
events.blurb: A prolonged drought and record heat fueled a six-month season of bushfires that burned 24 million hectares of southeastern Australia — an area larger than England. 33 people died directly; several hundred more from smoke. An estimated one billion wild animals perished. Smoke drifted across the Pacific and circled the globe.
events.revealBlurb: September 2019 – March 2020 — Australia. Images of koalas drinking from cyclists' water bottles and a town sheltering under blood-red skies went viral. Firefighters came from 12 countries. The season ended just as COVID-19 lockdowns began, compounding public trauma.

events.title: Stockton & Darlington Railway Opens
events.blurb: A steam locomotive hauling 21 coal wagons and one passenger coach completed a 40-kilometre journey through County Durham at a top speed of 24 km/h, carrying 450 passengers on its inaugural run. It was the first railway to carry both freight and fare-paying passengers using steam traction.

events.title: Faraday Demonstrates Induction
events.blurb: A 40-year-old self-taught English scientist, working in a London institution's basement, wrapped an iron ring with two coils of insulated wire, connected one coil to a battery and the other to a galvanometer, and observed that momentarily closing or opening the battery circuit caused a pulse of current in the other coil. The discovery — electromagnetic induction — was the foundation principle of every electrical generator and transformer ever built.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 1831 — Michael Faraday at the Royal Institution. He had been a bookbinder's apprentice with barely any formal schooling; Humphry Davy hired him as a lab assistant and he eclipsed his mentor. He was offered a knighthood twice and the presidency of the Royal Society; he refused both.

events.title: Drake Strikes Oil
events.blurb: A former railroad conductor, working on behalf of a small Pennsylvania oil-extraction company, struck oil at a depth of 21 metres while drilling a well using salt-drilling techniques borrowed from Chinese craftsmen. The well produced about 25 barrels a day — at the time, world-altering. Within two years, western Pennsylvania had hundreds of wells; within twenty, American oil companies were exporting kerosene around the world; within fifty, petroleum had overtaken coal as the premier industrial fuel.
events.revealBlurb: August 27, 1859 — Edwin Drake at Titusville, Pennsylvania. Drake himself died poor; he had failed to patent his drilling-pipe innovations. John D. Rockefeller entered the Cleveland refining business five years later and, with Standard Oil, came to dominate the industry within a decade.

events.title: Edison's Practical Lightbulb
events.blurb: After 14 months of systematic experimentation with thousands of possible filament materials — and many previous lightbulb designs by other inventors — an American inventor's laboratory team achieved a 40-hour burn using a carbonized cotton-thread filament in an evacuated glass bulb. The achievement's significance was not inventing the lightbulb itself (which had existed in various forms for decades) but making one that burned long enough to be commercially viable.
events.revealBlurb: October 21, 1879 — Thomas Edison at Menlo Park. His 1880 improved version used a bamboo filament and burned 1,200 hours. Edison's real genius was less invention than the systematic industrial R&D lab he created — the template for every modern corporate research operation.

events.title: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.blurb: Two American bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft on a windswept dune at the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — about the wingspan of a modern commercial airliner. They made three more flights that morning; the fourth covered 260 metres in 59 seconds. Few newspapers reported the achievement; commercial aviation took another three decades to arrive.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1903 — Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, NC. The flyer is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. The pair spent 4 years after their first flight battling patent disputes and litigation rather than manufacturing planes.

events.title: Cabbage Patch Kids Craze
events.blurb: Mass-marketed soft dolls with distinctive rotund faces, each shipped with an individual "birth certificate" and name, became the must-have Christmas gift of the holiday shopping season in the United States. Retail stampedes, fights, and injuries were reported as parents competed to buy the limited supplies of the dolls — Coleco had grossly underestimated demand. Adjusted for population, Cabbage Patch Kids may have sold more units in their peak years than any toy ever.
events.revealBlurb: December 1983 — Coleco. Xavier Roberts had been selling hand-sewn versions ("Little People") at craft fairs for years before the mass-market deal. Riots and fights occurred at multiple US stores; Coleco sold about 3 million dolls in 1983 and 20 million by the end of 1984.

events.title: Madonna's "Like a Prayer" Video
events.blurb: The music video for a 30-year-old singer's new single, featuring burning crosses, stigmata, and the singer kissing a Black saint statue coming to life, premiered during a Pepsi commercial at the start of a television special paid for by the soft-drink company. The Vatican condemned the video as blasphemous; conservative Christian groups organized boycotts; Pepsi paid the singer $5 million to sever their sponsorship deal. Her album sold 15 million copies.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1989 — the Pepsi commercial; the full video premiered on MTV March 3. Director Mary Lambert. The controversy gave Madonna an estimated $5 million for the Pepsi deal plus enormous free publicity; she kept the money. The album "Like a Prayer" remains her best-reviewed.

events.title: The Simpsons Premieres
events.blurb: A half-hour animated primetime sitcom about a dysfunctional yellow-skinned family in the fictional American town of Springfield premiered as a Christmas special on a fledgling US television network. The show's acerbic satire, cartoon slapstick, and unprecedented crossover appeal — with children and adults watching together — established animation as a legitimate prime-time format. It is still in production three and a half decades later, the longest-running American scripted prime-time TV series.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1989 — the Christmas special "Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire" on the Fox network. Created by Matt Groening from shorts he had been making for The Tracey Ullman Show since 1987. The family was named after Groening's own family except Bart, an anagram of "brat."

events.title: Princess Diana Dies
events.blurb: A 36-year-old former British princess and two others died in a high-speed car crash in an underpass in central Paris after their driver attempted to evade pursuing paparazzi. Her death — ten months after her divorce from the heir to the British throne — triggered a massive public outpouring of grief that caught the British monarchy off guard. Over a million bouquets of flowers were left at London's royal palaces. Her funeral a week later was watched by 2.5 billion people globally.
events.revealBlurb: August 31, 1997 — Diana, Princess of Wales at the Pont de l'Alma tunnel. Her companion Dodi Fayed and the drunk driver Henri Paul also died; bodyguard Trevor Rees-Jones survived. Elton John performed a rewritten "Candle in the Wind" at the funeral, which became the best-selling single of all time.

events.title: South Park Premieres
events.blurb: An animated half-hour adult-comedy series about four foul-mouthed 8-year-old boys in a small Colorado mountain town premiered on the Comedy Central cable network. The deliberately crude cut-paper animation style and its topical-to-the-minute production timeline (each episode was produced in a week rather than the months typical for animation) gave it a reactive speed no other animated show could match. It would remain in production for over 25 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1997 — created by Trey Parker and Matt Stone. Their earlier Christmas short, "The Spirit of Christmas," had circulated as a VHS among Hollywood executives in 1995. The show's 1999 feature film nearly received an NC-17 rating; the MPAA gave it R after the creators submitted it six times.
